title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on alleged espionage
excerpt:
The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in the far eastern region of Sakhalin

Russian authorities have charged a Japanese journalist for espionage, accusing hi...
body_text:
The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in the far eastern region of Sakhalin

Russian authorities have charged a Japanese journalist for espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.

The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in Russia's far eastern region of Sakhalin, a day before he was due to leave the country.

The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands, claimed by both countries, in August.

Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities are "verifying the facts" and will "respond appropriately" thereafter.

Russian authorities allege that Imai had "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported.

The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories.

Imai has been taken to Moscow and will be remanded until 12 December, before the trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency.

Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be jailed up to 20 years in prison.

"Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday.

"We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity.

Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin.

Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter, but did not comment further on the incident.

Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two.

Takaichi slammed Putin's visit in August – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories".

Moscow dismissed her criticism as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded".

Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo for requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese.

The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine.

In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

Gershkovich, a US citizen, was in 2024 released in a prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War took place.

In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours.

title: Court overturns Tanya Plibersek’s protection order which stalled controversial NSW goldmine
excerpt:
Federal court overrules decision by former environment minister for the McPhillamys goldmine development at Blayney

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news ...
body_text:
Federal court overrules decision by former environment minister for the McPhillamys goldmine development at Blayney

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The federal court has overturned a rare protection order issued by former environment minister Tanya Plibersek under Indigenous heritage legislation, which the company said effectively blocked a goldmine in the central west of New South Wales.

Regis Resources challenged the decision by the former minister to issue the order in 2024 under section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act.

The Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation asked the minister to protect the headwaters and the springs of the Belubula River as a site central to creation stories.

The company said at the time the protection order, while affecting only part of the site and not the area intended to be mined, would make its McPhillamys goldmine development at Blayney unviable.

The order blocked the company from building a tailings dam in the headwaters of the Belubula River.

In a decision on Wednesday morning, Justice James Stellios ruled the order was invalid. The reasons for the court’s decision will be published on Friday.

According to the ABC, Stellios said on Wednesday the court’s decision and his reasons “say nothing about the merits of the claim … whether it’s a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration … those are matters within the authority of the minister … not the jurisdiction of this court.”

At a three-day hearing last year, Regis Resources argued it had been denied procedural fairness and the government made errors in the process it followed before issuing the protection order.

The company’s lawyer, Perry Herzfeld SC, argued a blue-banded bee Dreaming story that influenced the government’s decision to protect the area was not raised until two years after the initial application for a section 10 order was made.

In a statement, the company said it anticipated the current environment minister, Murray Watt, “will be required to redetermine the application for a Section 10 Declaration, having regard to the relevant findings made by Justice Stellios in the judgment”.

“Today’s federal court judgment is a significant and welcome step forward for the McPhillamys Gold Project,” managing director Jim Beyer said.

“The judgment finding that the Section 10 Declaration is legally invalid vindicates the position we have held since the Declaration was made in August 2024, and we are extremely pleased the Court has agreed.”

Watt said the government respected the court’s decision.

“I note the judge specifically made the point that his decision did not concern the merits of the minister’s decision. Instead, the court’s decision was based on an error in the process used to grant the declaration,” he said.

He said the government was carefully considering the judgment and taking advice on next steps.

“We understand this outcome will matter deeply to the Wiradyuri Elders who brought the application, as well as to the company and its workforce, and to the Blayney community. We’ll work through it as quickly as possible.”

Regis Resources said because any process to redetermine the protection order application could be protracted and “or for the outcome not to be in Regis’ favour”, the company was still pursing an alternative approach to the development.

The company said that plan would involve co-disposal of filtered processed ore and waste rock into a single facility – referred to as an Integrated Waste Landform – “and entirely avoids the area impacted by the declaration”.

“After considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost, we are eager to move forward,” Beyer said.

“We look forward to engaging constructively with the Department through the redetermination process, and to advance one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects – one with the potential to deliver lasting economic and social benefits to the Central New South Wales region and our broader stakeholder community.”

New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, said in 2024 he was disappointed the protection order was issued and believed the federal minister’s decision was an error.

Before the court’s decision on Wednesday morning, Minns said he wanted the mine to proceed.

“I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment.

“There are more people in mining jobs in New South Wales today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that. It’s a really important part of our economy.”

Watt said the court’s findings were an example “how complex the current cultural heritage processes are for everyone involved”.

“First Nations people, industry and State and Territory governments have been clear with us for some time that they feel the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection (ATSIHP) Act doesn’t give enough certainty,” he said.

“We remain committed to working alongside them on a better system.”

The Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC), which supported the heritage protection order application, said while it was disappointed by the court’s decision, it respected the judicial process.

A spokesperson said the corporation would review the judgment “and its implications for Wiradyuri people, our cultural heritage, and the ongoing protection of Country”.

“This case has always been about protecting places of profound cultural and spiritual significance to Wiradyuri people,” they said.

“The areas covered by the protection declaration, including the headwaters of the Belubula River, remain deeply important to our community and to the continuation of cultural knowledge, practices, and responsibilities that have been maintained for countless generations.

“The court’s decision does not diminish the cultural significance of these places, nor does it alter our obligation to speak for and care for Country.”

title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post
excerpt:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year

Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentence...
body_text:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year

Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post.

Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.

A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet).

In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.

Amini was arrested by security forces during January’s nationwide protests, which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.

In an audio recording released from the prison last month, Amini appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.

“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.

“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” Amini said. “I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning.”

Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini’s case should be seen as a serious warning.

“Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further,” he said.

Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community’s “tolerance” towards capital punishment. “If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common,” he said.

Under article 262 of Iran’s Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.

According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends and her defence argued it was a “slip of the tongue”.

The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: “Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?”

Amini’s death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran’s supreme court.

The student’s sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking to criminalise contact with all foreign media, including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.

Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.

“I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it’s not just the regime’s cyber-police we have to worry about. There’s also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I’m alone in my room.

“I’m scared to post anything on social media … but after everything they’ve put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don’t post anything on social media.”

Although executions in Iran have surged in recent years, reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.

* Name has been changed to protect her identity

title: Ukraine is littered with landmines on a scale last seen in Vietnam. How can they be removed?
excerpt:
Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI

Crouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging into the gr...
body_text:
Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI

Crouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging into the ground. With a shovel and a steady hand, the 58-year-old digs out a neat square around the spot where a mine detector has sensed a suspicious object.

Four years ago, this field in eastern Ukraine was occupied by Russian soldiers. Now back under Ukrainian control, it is littered with landmines. Civilians such as Kabanova are trying to make the land usable again.

Landmines are a scourge of conflict zones. Littered across contested territory, they leave land unusable for years after a war has ended. Removing them is an expensive and dangerous job. And the use of long-range drones in Ukraine, which is often described as the most mine-contaminated country in the world, is increasing the scale of the problem.

“What we’re now seeing is the massive increase in the use of drone-delivered munitions,” says Paul Heslop, the programme manager for mine action at the United Nations Development Programme in Ukraine. “What already was a very high-intensity battle area is now potentially, through the use of drones on both sides, becoming a much wider area of contamination and a scale that we haven’t seen since the Americans were dropping cluster munitions on the Ho Chi Minh trail.”

The task of clearing landmines from Ukraine is replete with challenges. Drone and missile attacks make working outdoors unsafe; humanitarian workers are sometimes directly targeted. And newer, deadlier threats are also appearing. They include the POM-3, a small cylindrical mine used by Russian forces that could be mistaken for an abandoned vacuum flask. It is detonated by the vibrations of approaching footsteps.

POM-3 mines mean there are “specific villages that we just completely avoid”, says Anda Riza, a unit commander of the Halo Trust, the largest international humanitarian demining organisation in Ukraine, which employs Kabanova in the field in Kharkiv. The types of landmines are “constantly developing and evolving”, says Valeriia Shumska, Riza’s colleague.

But the technological innovation that is emerging from the conflict is also helping deminers to come up with new ways of working, which they hope are quicker and safer than the traditional hands-and-knees approach. The advances are being supported by the $1.5bn funding that has poured into Ukraine’s demining sector since the start of the full-scale invasion.

Take Kabanova’s job. Digging out a patch of land could take up to 45 minutes. But a new machine can do it in five. Called the DMR-7, it is a small, tank-like vehicle fitted with a hosepipe that shoots out jet flows of compressed air.

The tank is operated by a human using a remote controller who stands at a safe distance away. The operator manoeuvres the tank into place and then, with a loud mechanical whirring and plumes of dirt billowing skywards, the DMR-7 uses the force of compressed air to blast away a small patch of soil. It is a bulky, expensive alternative to a shovel, but it’s one that deminers hope can make one of the most dangerous parts of the demining process quicker and safer.

The DMR-7 is just one of a host of new pieces of kit that the Halo Trust is experimenting with in Ukraine. Other technologies include AI-powered image analysis, ground-penetrating radar and devices that can detect explosive material, not just metal.

Just as drones have transformed the battlefield, they have also created new opportunities for humanitarians. Before 2022, much of Halo’s surveillance work – looking for signs of explosives – was done with binoculars and maps. Now it is done with drones, and satellite imagery, which can be analysed with the help of AI.

But war has also led to innovations in anti-drone technology. Drone jamming systems, used by both Russian and Ukrainian forces, can interfere with humanitarian work. Halo has lost several drones to jamming and spoofing attacks.

And the advances in new technology are not spread equally between providers.

In a field adjacent to one that Kabanova is working in, staff from the state emergency services are also clearing mines. Under the glare of the late summer sun, Mykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit, says his colleagues have started using drones for surveillance. But they are not yet able to use AI to analyse the drone-captured imagery. “I really hope this kind of technology will be implemented soon in our work,” he says.

The Halo Trust alone spent nearly £50m in Ukraine in the year to 31 March 2025, dwarfing the state’s annual budget of £28.6m for a programme to clear agricultural land of mines and unexploded ordnance. And there are dozens of other demining organisations with overlapping responsibilities and approaches. Responsibility for the sector is split across multiple government agencies. Attempts to reform the country’s mine action law to bring it in line with international standards have faltered.

Ihor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister who leads the country’s work on demining, wants to streamline the policymaking process to create one cabinet-level office to oversee the whole sector. But progress has been slow. Asked why, he offers a weary shrug: “Because, people.”

“When we’re talking about a new law, it will mean that some government bodies will lose responsibility, and, they think, power,” Bezkaravainyi says.

One person who has worked in Ukraine’s demining sector puts it more bluntly: “The biggest barrier to demining Ukraine is the government of Ukraine.”

Bezkaravainyi says: “When we’re talking about an ordinary situation with mine action … the conflict has ended, and the government does not exist … in Ukraine, it’s the opposite situation.”

That leads to a host of regulatory and bureaucratic barriers. For example, deminers are often prevented from using vehicles that are driven directly by a person, with health and safety standards requiring that the vehicles are operated remotely. Riza says: “We know for a fact that doing it remotely is much slower than having a person in the cab. That continues to be our biggest challenge.”

Heslop argues that the Ukrainian authorities are overly broad in their categorisation of land as being contaminated by mines, an approach that risks wasting time and money on clearing land that wasn’t dangerous in the first place. “Just because it was occupied by the Russians doesn’t necessarily mean it was contaminated,” he says. “Land is only contaminated if it’s got fucking explosives in it.”

But deminers across the sector agree that technological advances will accelerate their ability to release Ukraine’s richly fertile land for civilian use at a much faster rate than has been possible in the past.

“This is the cutting edge of technology,” says Heslop. “This is where the humanitarian mine action sector is going through the biggest pivot in the last 30 years.”

Additional research by Illia Dyadik and Artem Mazhulin

title: UN official says ‘window of opportunity’ for peace in DR Congo
excerpt: A senior United Nations official has told the Security Council there is a “window of opportunity” for peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a mineral-rich region plagued by decades of...
body_text:
A senior United Nations official has told the Security Council there is a “window of opportunity” for peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a mineral-rich region plagued by decades of conflict.

Huang Xia, the UN special envoy for the impacted Great Lakes Region, on Tuesday said that both US- and Qatar-led peace processes have achieved “notable progress”.

However, “despite this sustained diplomatic effort, the security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has continued to worsen”, he added.

Several parties, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group and the Congolese army, have clashed in the territory, prompting a series of international diplomatic efforts.

Huang stressed the “urgency of seizing the window of opportunity, which is currently offered by the increased alignment of peace efforts”.

“Such a window does not remain open indefinitely,” he said.

“I therefore urge all parties to translate commitments into verifiable actions, and to place their trust in confidence built through deeds rather than through declarations.”

The Congolese government and the M23 signed a commitment towards a ceasefire in Doha in July 2025. The DRC and Rwanda also formalised a US-brokered peace deal in December in Washington, DC.

However, fighting has continued on the ground.

New talks were held in August in Switzerland, involving representatives from the United States, Qatar and the African Union.

Huang said the UN would facilitate a meeting on October 18 in Zambia’s capital, Lusaka, between the defence ministers of Burundi, the DRC, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania.

title: Family of Indigenous woman found dead in Melbourne mourn ‘vibrant, beautiful young girl’
excerpt:
Police have charged a 31-year-old man with the alleged murder of Jayda Allen Bonner, whose body was found in a Carlton apartment on Saturday

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest update...
body_text:
Police have charged a 31-year-old man with the alleged murder of Jayda Allen Bonner, whose body was found in a Carlton apartment on Saturday

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Warning: This article contains images of and references to Indigenous Australians who have died

The family of a young Indigenous woman found dead in an apartment complex in Melbourne’s inner-north on Saturday say they are “absolutely crushed and shattered” by her death.

Jayda Allen Bonner, 21, was found dead on the fifth floor of an apartment block on Cardigan Street, Carlton on Saturday at about 1.45am.

Police on Wednesday charged a 31-year-old man with murder. He was expected to appear in the Melbourne magistrates court that afternoon.

The man presented himself at a police station on Monday, police said.

A 60-year-old man who was initially arrested has been released without charge.

Bonner’s aunt, Kellie Carter-Bell described her niece as a “vibrant, beautiful young girl” who was “fed to the wolves because the system didn’t listen”.

Carter-Bell said Bonner had been with her partner, who was 10 years her senior, since she was 15 years old.

Bonner lived with Carter-Bell in Melbourne as a young child and attended school in Carlton.

Her aunt said “she was a beautiful family girl”, who had hopes of moving back to Queensland to be with “her mob and to work in the community”.

“Jayda wanted to share her own knowledge of what she could [do] to help her community,” she said. “I’ve heard from her school teachers what a beautiful, vibrant young lady she was.

“She had a lot of dreams and aspirations … She looks exactly like her mother, which is beautiful.

“She’s someone this world shouldn’t have lost.

“I couldn’t save my niece, so I feel worthless and useless at the moment.

“The family is absolutely crushed and shattered. We don’t want her to ever be forgotten.”

title: Jim Chalmers denies Anthony Albanese rolled him over credit card payments for tax bills
excerpt:
Treasurer’s comments come after prime minister revealed he intervened to delay a controversial ban on such payments to the ATO

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our new...
body_text:
Treasurer’s comments come after prime minister revealed he intervened to delay a controversial ban on such payments to the ATO

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has denied being rolled by Anthony Albanese after the prime minister personally intervened to stop a tax office ban on credit card payments a day before stopgap funding was announced.

After sustained criticism of the government’s handling of the ban on tax bills being paid by credit card, Chalmers last week announced new funding for the ATO to ensure card payments could continue until the end of the financial year.

Albanese has since revealed he acted after discussions with Andrew McKellar, the boss of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), earlier than previously known, prompting suggestions Albanese had undermined Chalmers.

But, when asked if he had been rolled, Chalmers denied the prime minister went over his head to intervene on the ATO’s decision to ban credit card payments.

“If you just let me set it out for you, [the] prime minister and I were in discussions on Wednesday of last week,” he said on Wednesday morning.

“He had a view and I agree with it, that we needed to step in to provide this longer transition period to allow the ATO the time to get it right. We had the same view.”

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese said at Parliament House on Tuesday night that he acted when concerns were raised with him.

“Andrew [McKellar] did text me last Thursday morning and by Friday morning we had an announcement,” he said.

“That was an example of a relationship that takes time to develop. That trust, where you can have a discussion and say ‘it is in hand, I agree with what you are saying and I will get it done’.”

The tax commissioner, Rob Heferen, announced earlier this month that the ATO would stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from 1 December. The move followed a ban on surcharges announced by the Reserve Bank.

Heferen said continuing to accept card payments would cost the ATO almost $200m a year, as those costs could not legally be passed on to card users.

But some business owners, particularly smaller operators, use credit card payments as a cashflow tool, managing their liabilities by using credit when required. Estimates suggest about 5% of small businesses use credit card payments for tax bills.

The ATO is an independent authority and the government cannot direct the tax commissioner’s decisions.

Chalmers told ABC radio on Wednesday he was involved in the conversations with ACCI as well, describing the intervention as a joint decision with the prime minister.

“I have an open door. I’ve met with ACCI in recent weeks, in fact, and we were engaging on these issues as well,” he said.

He said he had discussions with Albanese last Wednesday, before he and the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, took a proposal to ministerial colleagues.

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, told News24 the intervention was more evidence of Albanese overriding Chalmers.

“The prime minister has a kink for punishing small businesses and a fetish for humiliating his treasurer,” he said.

“So I say this is a consistent pattern of behaviour where the prime minister constantly goes in, overrides his treasurer, humiliates him in public. I suspect it’s going to sour the relationship somewhat.”

title: Panic in Dallas: Cowboys defense holds emergency summit as season spirals after Bucs loss
excerpt: Dan reacts to one of the wildest, most chaotic weekends of college football in recent memory—and explains why Coach Curt Cignetti has officially ruined patience for every athletic director and booster...
body_text:
Dan reacts to one of the wildest, most chaotic weekends of college football in recent memory—and explains why Coach Curt Cignetti has officially ruined patience for every athletic director and booster in the country.

Five weeks into the season and fresh off an embarrassing loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Dallas Cowboys are already breaking out the oldest crisis gimmick in football: the defensive players-only meeting.

Sitting at 2-3 and watching their defense get pushed around on a weekly basis, the entire unit gathered behind closed doors on Monday morning to air out their issues.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Cowboys LB DeMarvion Overshown described the session as a blunt "heart-to-heart."

Quinnen Williams No. 92 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on from the field during an NFL game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

Yaya Diaby of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers rushes the passer during an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

"Looking ourselves in the mirror," Overshown said.

"Putting what we wanted our standard to be, we put that on the board. We went by bullet point, bullet point. Are we holding up to this? Are we being this? As a unit, how can we get closer? What is it? Just hearing from all of us. It really wasn't like a fire drill conversation, it was more so, 'What can I do to help you? What do I expect from you on Sundays, or every Monday walk throughs?' We've got to talk to each other like that because the ship is only going to go as far as the weakest person on the boat. As long as we all in this together, I think we're going to be great. I know we're going to be there."

JERRY JONES SLAMS TABLE AFTER DAK PRESCOTT THROWS CRITICAL LATE INTERCEPTION IN BRUTAL COWBOYS LOSS

Writing bullet points on a dry-erase board is cute, but it does not erase what happened against Tampa Bay.

Dallas got thoroughly embarrassed at home by a winless Buccaneers squad, surrendering 241 rushing yards and making an 0-4 offense look explosive.

Dak Prescott No. 4 of the Dallas Cowboys warms up before a game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium on Oct. 8, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. (Getty Images)

Tyler Goodson No. 32 of the Dallas Cowboys runs out of the tunnel before an NFL game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium on Oct. 8, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. (Getty Images)

The Cowboys surrendered 419 total yards, blew basic run fits, and failed to force a single takeaway. Through five weeks, Dallas has surrendered at least 375 yards every game. Management is now scrambling to stop the bleeding before a tough road trip to Green Bay.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Defensive coordinator Christian Parker is moving upstairs to the coaching booth, and longtime NFL coach Mike Pettine was hired as a senior assistant to provide adult supervision.

Meanwhile, Dallas hopes Overshown's return from a four-game hamstring injury adds badly needed speed.

Whiteboard therapy is fine, but unless this group starts tackling someone, the Cowboys' season is officially cooked.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Man who lived as woman for eight years warns surprising teen sexuality data may not tell full story
excerpt: Walt Heyer tells Fox News Digital why he believes social media and peer pressure may influence how teenagers identify their sexual orientation, urging more research before drawing conclusions from new...
body_text:
Walt Heyer tells Fox News Digital why he believes social media and peer pressure may influence how teenagers identify their sexual orientation, urging more research before drawing conclusions from new data.

A man who spent eight years identifying as a woman is casting doubt on reports of a dramatic decline in teenagers identifying as gay or bisexual, warning that social media and peer pressure may be influencing how young Americans describe their sexual orientation.

Walt Heyer, who detransitioned roughly 40 years ago and now serves as a senior fellow at the Family Research Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive video interview that he remains skeptical of the apparent shift, suggesting some teenagers may be reluctant to openly identify as gay or bisexual because of social pressures.

"I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall," Heyer said, referring to recent reports about declining rates of gay and bisexual identification among some teenagers.

LOG CABIN REPUBLICANS REMOVES 'T' FROM LGBT ADVOCACY, SAYS 'RADICAL' TRANS ACTIVISTS ARE ERODING GAY SUPPORT

Walt Heyer lived as a woman for eight years named "Laura Jensen," before returning to live as a man. (Walt Heyer)

"I think what's happening is that because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual, but really don't want to openly admit it," Heyer said.

The comments come after The Washington Post highlighted CDC data showing that the percentage of ninth-grade girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual fell from 30% in 2021 to 17% in 2025. The share identifying as bisexual alone dropped from 26% to 13% over the same period.

PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME

The percentage of boys identifying as gay or bisexual has remained pretty much unchanged over the past decade, according to CDC data reported by The Washington Post. (iStock)

The percentage of boys identifying as gay or bisexual has remained largely unchanged over the past decade, while the share of high school girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual surged following the COVID-19 pandemic before beginning to decline, the Post reported.

Heyer, an author and co-author of multiple books including "Trans Life Survivors" and "Paper Genders" who has spent years working with people questioning their gender identities, argued that social dynamics among young people could complicate attempts to interpret the findings.

"I've had actual people in school saying that they're bullied into identifying one way, or they're bullying and bullied to not identify that way," he said.

BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

Detransitioner Walt Heyer was skeptical of data showing fewer teens identified as LGBTQ in 2025, citing the influence of social media and peer pressure. (iStock)

Heyer also said he believes peer and societal pressures are significant factors in kids choosing to identify with something else that is not their biological sex.

"What's interesting about that is that many kids are sort of coerced by their peers to say things one way or the other, so I've been very skeptical about what the kids are saying, whether they're gay or bisexual," Heyer said.

"I don't really believe that there's a big dramatic free fall. That was, I think, quoted as a free fall in the people identifying as gay or bisexual," he added. "I think what's happening is that, because of social media, there's a lot more influence on people who may not want to fall into that classification on a social media level and will withhold the fact that they are gay or bisexual, but really don't want to openly admit it."

A DETRANSITIONER CONFRONTED A CALIFORNIA LAWMAKER ON THE HARMS OF GENDER TRANSITION. HERE'S WHY HE SPOKE OUT

Walt Heyer works with individuals struggling with gender identity. (iStock)

Simply but perhaps most importantly, Heyer said he thinks adults should do a better job of only affirming what is true.

"I think that what I've really discovered is that we know now and have evidence, factual evidence, that nobody has ever changed their gender," Heyer said. "I went through the hormones, had all the surgeries, identified that way. So far in all world history, nobody has actually biologically changed their gender. This is a cosmetic social appearance, it is not a biological change."

"And when you come to that conclusion, you realize that really the procedures and these terminologies and labels, what I refer to as God rejecting labels, God rejecting procedures in every aspect. This is the way young people and adults reject God and say God doesn't exist by taking these labels on," he added.

DETRANSITIONERS REVEAL HOW DOCTORS PUSHED THEM TOWARD LIFE-ALTERING TREATMENT AS TEENS

Walt Heyer, who spent eight years identifying as a woman, now spends his life helping others who are confused about their gender accept biological reality. (Courtesy of Walt Heyer)

Heyer also urged researchers to conduct additional studies before concluding that the numbers reflect a lasting shift in sexual identity.

"I just think it's important for us to be much more thorough and go to other areas before we come to some conclusion that there's a giant, giant drop in these identities," he said. "I don't think we're there yet."

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

title: Former Chicago police detective linked by DNA to 8-year-old girl's cold-case murder, police say
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former Chicago homicide detective has been identified as the killer of an 8-year-old girl who disappeared while walk...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A former Chicago homicide detective has been identified as the killer of an 8-year-old girl who disappeared while walking to church in 1960, with authorities now examining other cases that may have involved the officer.

Thomas F. McInerney Jr. joined the Chicago Police Department in 1959, just one year before Gloria Kowalewicz was abducted and murdered. He later became a detective investigating violent crimes and remained with the department until retiring in 1987.

More than 65 years after the killing, Chicago police confirmed to Fox News Digital that advances in DNA technology and a preserved fingerprint helped investigators identify McInerney, who died in 2006 at age 70.

COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID'

A Chicago Police Department building. Police identified a former department detective as the killer of 8-year-old Gloria Kowalewicz, who was murdered in 1960. (Getty Images)

Gloria disappeared Nov. 12, 1960, after leaving her home shortly before 8 a.m. to attend morning Mass at St. Mary of Mt. Carmel Church, just a few blocks away. Her body was discovered roughly four hours later in a ditch at a forest preserve southwest of Chicago. She had been shot and killed.

The murder prompted an extensive investigation, with police interviewing more than 1,300 people and knocking on hundreds of doors. Despite those efforts, the case remained unsolved for decades.

Investigators preserved evidence from the crime scene and surrounding area, including a bullet, Gloria's coat and shoes, and a white communion purse containing her prayer book. A fingerprint was also recovered from the purse's strap.

DISCARDED TRASH UNCAPS 41-YEAR-OLD MURDER CASE IN RITZY SEASIDE RESORT TOWN, AUTHORITIES SAY

Staff prepare samples for DNA sequencing at the new offices and laboratories of Othram, a DNA forensics lab, in The Woodlands, Texas, on Nov. 6, 2023. (Michael Wyke/Houston Chronicle)

Working with the FBI and Illinois State Police, investigators used modern forensic technology to link DNA and the preserved fingerprint to McInerney, according to the department.

"McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive," Chicago police said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

The Cook County State's Attorney's Office is working to identify other cases that may have involved McInerney, according to The Associated Press.

KILLER EX-COP EXECUTED FOR CHILD'S SLAYING AS SHERIFF SAYS HE’S SURE SAME MONSTER MURDERED ANOTHER GIRL

The Chicago Police Department said DNA evidence and a preserved fingerprint helped investigators identify the killer of 8-year-old Gloria Kowalewicz more than 65 years after her murder. (Talia Sprague/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Police said Gloria's parents died before learning who killed their daughter, but expressed hope that identifying McInerney would bring some closure to those who knew her.

McInerney later worked for the Federal Public Defender's Office in Nevada before retiring in 2004, according to the AP. He died two years later without facing charges in Gloria's murder.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: OpenAI engineer charged after listening device found in meeting room
excerpt: A Saudi national who worked as an engineer at the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI has been arrested after a listening device was found in the company’s conference room, according to United States ...
body_text:
A Saudi national who worked as an engineer at the artificial intelligence firm OpenAI has been arrested after a listening device was found in the company’s conference room, according to United States authorities.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Department of Justice said that the employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi engineer named Abdulrahman Alfozan, had worked at the company since July 2025.

Prosecutors accused Alfozan of using the listening device to illegally obtain sensitive information.

Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday and faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Kash Patel, the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in response to the arrest.

The incident raises concerns about surveillance and underhanded efforts to gain an edge in the AI sector, where companies and countries have angled for an advantage.

A Justice Department complaint said that the device, concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28 and discovered on September 30.

Prosecutors explained that video surveillance from OpenAI’s offices showed Alfozan appearing near the executive conference room on multiple dates before the device was discovered, despite having no authority to access the room or participate in its meetings. Such meetings, they added, were highly confidential.

OpenAI security personnel also reportedly found a second listening device in Alfozan’s bag.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code or customer data,” OpenAI said in a social media post. “The employee was terminated.”

The company also said it used its own AI models to identify the person allegedly responsible for planting the device.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” the company said.

“We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.”

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.

title: Joe Manganiello's secret seven-year health battle that nearly killed him
excerpt:
‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital if she would ever set up Sofia Vergara on a date.

Joe Manganiello is opening up about the secret health battle that nearly "took his lif...
body_text:
‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital if she would ever set up Sofia Vergara on a date.

Joe Manganiello is opening up about the secret health battle that nearly "took his life" over 7 years.

Manganiello sat down with "CBS Mornings" to discuss his health and his newly released memoir, "Bloodlines." During his appearance, the actor told Gayle King that he was offered the role as the main villain, Deathstroke, in Ben Affleck's canceled "Batman" movie.

He wrote in his memoir that at the same time as the job offer, he was "dying." Manganiello received the call to appear in the movie in 2016.

Joe Manganiello had to have his entire large intestine removed to save his life in 2016. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"I got the call about a month out of the hospital after I collapsed on another set," Manganiello told King. "After about a year of feeling these mystery symptoms, I went into the hospital for two months straight and at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life."

JOE MANGANIELLO DENIES SOFIA VERGARA’S CLAIM MARRIAGE ENDED BECAUSE HE WANTED A BABY: ‘SIMPLY NOT TRUE’

"They had split me open. My entire large intestine had turned to pus and it was about to explode," he continued. "They took it out and the surgery left me with an ostomy bag. And in the wake of that, I lost 60 pounds in two weeks. I couldn't walk. My eye went cross-eyed. I lost my voice. I had five catheters."

"I went into the hospital for two months straight and at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life."

Manganiello explained that after he was released from the hospital, he was in the process of trying to gain the weight back when he got the call to meet Affleck and appear in the "Batman" movie.

The actor told King that he was still married to Sofia Vergara at the time and she was the one who ultimately made the decision for the doctors to save his life and remove his large intestine.

Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello were married from 2015-2023. (WireImage)

"They had to call her as my next of kin and give her options of what she thought I would want done to me while I was unconscious. She chose the right one and it bought me time," Manganiello said. "It didn't solve the problem. The doctors still had know idea what was causing this, how to treat it, but it bought me enough time."

"But we do have to credit her for saving your life. For making that decision," King replied.

King went on to cite Manganiello's memoir where he wrote that his mystery illness put a strain on his marriage to Vergara. The former couple married in 2015 and announced their separation in 2023. Their divorce was finalized in 2024.

Joe Manganiello's "mystery illness" symptoms began shortly after he married Sofía Vergara. (FilmMagic)

"That kind of pain was like a flood in my life. You can't predict how that's going to affect people. It affected me a certain way, it affected her," he said. "It was seven years long. People didn't know about it. I was living in secret with this. Only the closest people around me knew."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

King mentioned that Vergara's son, Manolo Gonzalez Vergara, 35, shared a post about a "narcissistic" man on Monday.

Sofia Vergara's son, Manolo Gonzalez, allegedly shared a post that compared qualities of narcissistic men. (Christopher Polk/Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Her son posted a thing about, ‘This is what happens when you deal with a narcissistic man,’ and she has liked that post," King began. "They appear to be saying that basically, it’s terrible what happened to you but the bottom line is that you’re a narcissist. What do you say to that?"

Joe Manganiello has released his new memoir. (Michael Simon)

Manganiello appeared a bit shocked before he replied, "Well, I think anybody who said that should read the book first and understand what the book is actually about because it’s not about that. It’s about the suffering I went through."

"Bloodlines: A Memoir" released on Oct. 13.

title: Ex-gang leader gets 40 years to life for rapper Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
excerpt:
A former gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.

Tuesday’s sentencing capped a 30-year-long cold...
body_text:
A former gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.

Tuesday’s sentencing capped a 30-year-long cold case that rattled the golden era of rap music in the United States.

In August, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, had been found guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

Davis, 63, is the sole person charged in the death of Shakur, who died at the peak of his fame at age 25.

Judge Carli Kierny announced Davis’s sentence at a hearing in Las Vegas, Nevada, where she chided him for the murder.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family, you don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” Kierny said. “The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas.”

During the hearing, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.

For nearly three decades, Shakur’s death remained one of the music industry’s most notorious unsolved mysteries, prompting endless debate over who did it and why.

Davis had long been a suspect, but investigators lacked evidence to pursue an indictment.

The investigative deadlock shattered after Davis publicly boasted about his involvement in media interviews. He also recounted his role in the murder in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.

Previously, Davis entered into a 2008 proffer agreement with federal law enforcement officers, granting him limited immunity for statements he made privately to investigators.

But by repeating his statements outside his meetings with investigators, prosecutors said Davis had effectively voided the agreement’s protections.

DiGiacomo said that Davis was trying to profit from a killing that he committed, and for that, he deserves the maximum possible sentence.

Shakur had been in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight on the night of September 7, 1996, when he was shot.

Investigators said the shooting took place roughly two hours after a confrontation between Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, and Shakur’s entourage.

In his memoir, Davis accused Shakur and his friends of assaulting his nephew. He explained he then sought to retaliate, and he admitted to handing the murder weapon to two alleged accomplices, seated in the backseat of a white Cadillac, who then fired the fatal shots.

Shakur had been in the passenger seat of a black BMW, stopped at a red light, when his vehicle came under fire. He died six days later.

Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

Members of Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur.

“This man’s life mattered,” Sekyiwa Shakur told the court, while her brother called the murder “devastating, heartbreaking and sad”.

Following the verdict, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal described the Shakur family as having to endure years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”.

“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said.

The ex-gang leader briefly addressed the court on Tuesday, asking the judge to order the return of property seized from his residence, including personal photographs.

When the judge asked if he wished to make any additional statements, Davis declined, stating, “No, I’m good.” He added that he would “appeal this case for sure”.

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
excerpt:
Serhii K was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year

Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesd...
body_text:
Serhii K was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year

Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.

Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.

The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.

Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.

He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.

In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.

Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.

As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.

Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.

They said later that  "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".

Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022

Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".

They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects".

Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine

The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.

Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".

He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."

However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.

"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.

In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.

After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.

German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.

While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.

In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".

Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.

Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.

Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
excerpt:
Simbarashe Kundizeza says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles in Zimbabwe

Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelli...
body_text:
Simbarashe Kundizeza says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles in Zimbabwe

Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external.

The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.

"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme.

The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday.

It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.

Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.

The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external.

Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external.

Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.

"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external.

"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.

Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external.

In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.

Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.

She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".

Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".

"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."

Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".

In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to  English-language writing by non-native English speakers.

The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".

Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."

In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."

For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.

"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.

"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.

The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

"Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday.

On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write."

Africa basks in Booker boost for female writers

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: AI could make us increasingly stupid

Married couple win top African writing prize

body_text:
Dan reacts to one of the wildest, most chaotic weekends of college football in recent memory—and explains why Coach Curt Cignetti has officially ruined patience for every athletic director and booster in the country.

The NFL is expected to suspend Los Angeles Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson for two games after punching Buffalo Bills edge rusher Bradley Chubb after Monday night’s shootout and potential Super Bowl preview.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Footage of Jackson's tirade is indisputable, and the consequences are entirely self-inflicted. Monday night’s childish spectacle saw Jackson marching into the midfield, losing his cool, and throwing a bare-knuckle punch at Chubb. Jackson is expected to appeal the suspension.

The official suspension statement read, in part: "After the game, as players were shaking hands and exchanging jerseys, Jackson struck Buffalo linebacker Bradley Chubb in the face after a brief confrontation, violating Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship."

Alaric Jackson No. 77 of the Los Angeles Rams warms up before the game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo., on Sept. 27, 2026. (Getty Images)

Chubb, to his credit, took the higher road and kept his composure, letting Buffalo teammates pull him back, and allowed Jackson to bury himself on national television. He understood what Jackson couldn't: the cameras are running, and the bill always comes due.

RAMS OFFENSIVE LINEMAN PUNCHES BILLS LINEBACKER AFTER THRILLING GAME: 'TEMPERS GOT FLARED'

After the game, Chubb gave his reaction. "It's just emotions," he said, "They always catch the second guy. So, I let him swing. And then my teammates held me back, and I just chilled."

Chubb is a smart man; Jackson, not so much.

With Alaric Jackson, poor judgment is more of a pattern than a fluke.

Just four months ago, in June 2026, Jackson was arrested on charges of felony domestic violence in Southern California.

While prosecutors bypassed formal criminal charges in favor of a pre-filing diversion hearing, the incident remains subject to ongoing NFL review.

Alaric Jackson No. 77 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during training camp at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles, Calif., on July 31, 2026. (Getty Images)

In 2024, the league slapped Jackson with a two-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy after he recorded intimate encounters on his phone without consent, an incident that later triggered a civil lawsuit.

NFL FACING A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE EPIDEMIC THIS OFFSEASON WITH ARREST OF RAMS LINEMAN THE LATEST CASE

At some point, the headaches are eclipsing the talent. Rams coach Sean McVay preaches accountability and culture, yet his starting tackle keeps showcasing eye-rolling volatility.

The Rams sit at 2-3 in a tight NFC race, desperately needing stability to protect Matthew Stafford’s blind side. Jackson will be out of action when his team needs him most.

Alaric Jackson #77 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during the national anthem before an NFC Championship NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field in Seattle, Wash., on Jan. 25, 2026. (Getty Images)
