title: Potential Michigan serial killer may have left behind valuable evidence, former FBI profiler says
excerpt: Former senior FBI profiler Mary Ellen O'Toole joins 'The Big Weekend Show' to analyze the case and discuss the chilling similarities among the victims. Michigan State University ups its security as po...
body_text:
Former senior FBI profiler Mary Ellen O'Toole joins 'The Big Weekend Show' to analyze the case and discuss the chilling similarities among the victims. Michigan State University ups its security as police arrest a suspect in connection to one death.

A former FBI profiler warns that a potential serial killer in Michigan may have left behind valuable forensic evidence at outdoor crime scenes as authorities investigate whether five deaths in Lansing are connected.

Mary Ellen O'Toole told the "The Big Weekend Show" on Saturday that the killings posed risks for the offender because they occurred outdoors where the victims, all believed to have been homeless, were likely sleeping.

Two portions of the Lansing River Trail in Michigan are seen. Five deaths linked to the area over the last year have raised concerns that a potential serial killer may be stalking a popular recreation trail near Michigan State University. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

'UNMASKING A MONSTER': GOLDEN STATE KILLER SERIES CHALLENGES TIMELINE OF JOSEPH DEANGELO'S CRIMES

"It's also very high risk for the offender because the offender comes in to an open area and kills these people — and these are probably not quick homicides — and then has to leave the area."

"And I can almost tell you for sure that this offender is not cleaning up his crime scenes," she added. "So he's probably leaving behind some very valuable evidence for investigators to analyze."

Lansing Police Chief Rob Backus speaks about the string of recent deaths along the Lansing River Trail during a press conference on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, at police headquarters in downtown Lansing. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

FOX HOLLOW CORONER REVEALS WHY HE DOUBTS SUSPECTED SERIAL KILLER ACTED ALONE IN HUNT FOR ANSWERS

The five victims were discovered near the Lansing River Trail near Michigan State University. The deaths occurred between October 2025 and September 2026. Police arrested a suspect in connection with the stabbing death of one man, but have not linked him to the other deaths.

O'Toole said police have more work to do before determining whether the cases are related.

That includes examining unsolved homicides in the surrounding area and potentially other states for evidence of earlier crimes by the same offender.

"They'll look at other homicides both in Michigan and in the surrounding areas because we know from other cases serial killers can travel around, so they want to be able to understand the breadth and the extent of the damage that one person could do," she said.

"And in that effort, they'll be looking at what we call practice murders. These are the murders that a serial killer will engage in as they're becoming a lot better at their trade. And those practice murders could have occurred in Michigan or in another state," she added.

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

title: Hurricane Isaias’ devastating aftermath comes into focus in striking images
excerpt: United Cajun Navy Incident Cmdr. Josh Gill joins ‘Fox News Live’ as Florida communities begin cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias left widespread damage and power outages in its wake. Gill discusses re...
body_text:
United Cajun Navy Incident Cmdr. Josh Gill joins ‘Fox News Live’ as Florida communities begin cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias left widespread damage and power outages in its wake. Gill discusses recovery efforts on the ground and how volunteers are helping residents clear debris and rebuild after the storm.

Communities are beginning to assess the damage left behind by a powerful hurricane that tore through the region, leaving homes damaged, roads flooded and neighborhoods littered with debris.

Photos from some of the hardest-hit areas show the scale of the destruction as residents and emergency crews begin the long process of cleaning up and rebuilding.

HOW THE VIOLENT CATEGORY 2 STORM UNFOLDED ACROSS FLORIDA AND GULF COAST

Copper Brock helps salvage what he can from the Milton Quick Stop after the roof was torn off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Isaias slammed into the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, bringing destructive winds, dangerous storm surge and widespread flooding.

The hurricane tore roofs from buildings, uprooted trees and knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of customers across Florida and Alabama before pushing inland.

STUNNING FOOTAGE CAPTURES HURRICANE ISAIAS FROM INSIDE THE STORM’S EYE

In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

A home is partially destroyed after Hurricane Isaias came ashore. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Alex Dean cleans out his home that was severely damaged during Hurricane Isaias. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Isaias marked the first hurricane to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast since Hurricane Milton battered Florida in October 2024, nearly two years earlier.

The storm also became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, ending an unusually quiet stretch that saw no hurricanes develop until October.

DESANTIS DEPLOYS AN ARMY TO CLEAR ROADS, RESTORE POWER AFTER ISAIAS' LANDFALL

In an aerial view, a worker with Southern Land Services removes a tree that landed on a home when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

In an aerial view, a worker with Southern Land Services removes a tree that landed on a home when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Laura and Alex Dean clean out their home that was severely damaged during Hurricane Isaias. Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

As Isaias moved inland and weakened, the full extent of the hurricane's destruction began to emerge.

Stunning images from across the Gulf Coast capture what the powerful storm left behind.

In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Hurricane Isaias tore the siding off a home as it passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

A Shell gas station is collapsed after Hurricane Isaias came ashore.Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, October 9 along the U.S. Gulf coast. (Jen Golbeck/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Zelenskyy signals surprise at Trump claim of Russia-Ukraine ‘energy ceasefire’ but would back it if Moscow does – live updates
excerpt:
Ukraine’s president reportedly says Kyiv would accept a deal if Moscow does after US president posts announcement with no detail on social media

Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Ze...
body_text:
Ukraine’s president reportedly says Kyiv would accept a deal if Moscow does after US president posts announcement with no detail on social media

Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has discussed an energy ceasefire with the leaders of Canada, Finland and Nato and is awaiting details from the US.

Writing on X shortly after saying such a deal was “news to me”, the Ukrainian leader said:

double quotation mark“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it’s important for Russia to support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. From our Ukrainian side, there is always FULL support for de-escalation steps, protection of lives, and the necessary decisions to end the war and ensure lasting peace.”

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russia hit power plant ‘after’ Trump’s energy ceasefire statement.

The Ukrainian leader said he had briefed EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “on the brutal Russian strikes that continue unabated”.

“Just before our conversation, the Russians struck a power plant in Kyiv with a ‘shahed’ drone, and many districts experienced power outages. Later, there were strikes on energy facilities in the Kharkiv region.

“And all of this happened AFTER the President of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire”, he posted on X.

The US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe.

The US had made threats to cut off intelligence sharing and the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism for procuring US weapons for Ukraine, the officials added.
 “They are calling Kyiv . . . they are calling everyone [in Europe],” said an official who received a call from a US defence official.

In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump’s call for Zelensky to be replaced.

“I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president,” said 40-year-old local Olesia Goncharuk.

“We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people,” she told AFP.

The row between Zelensky and Trump comes weeks before closely-fought US elections dominated by voter frustration over the cost of living.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on ⁠Sunday in response to critical comments from US President Donald Trump that he will organize elections in Ukraine if ⁠Russian President Vladimir ⁠Putin agrees to ​a 60-day ceasefire.

“Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and ⁠we will organize elections,” Zelenskyy told ABC’s This Week programme.

Trump on Saturday criticized Zelenskyy for attacking Russian oil refineries a day after the ⁠US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive ​Moscow of revenues to fund its ‌war in Ukraine.

“I think ‌it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump had told ‌reporters at the White House.

In response, Zelenskyy said “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.

He said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel prices “when everybody in the world understands ‌because of the war in (the) Middle East, the prices are rising.“

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks ​on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and ⁠global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. ​The US exports ​about 1.5 million barrels of diesel ​per day.

Trump is under pressure to bring down rising ​fuel prices ahead of ‌November midterm ​elections that will ​determine whether his Republican Party will retain control of the US Congress for his final two years in office.

Many lawmakers, including Republicans, have criticized the diesel deal as rewarding Putin.

Russia’s military said on Sunday it had struck a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

A Russian Defence Ministry statement posted on Telegram said the logistics centre in the town of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the Ukrainian military.

It said the vessel was carrying a military cargo to the Black Sea port of Chernomorsk.

France backs a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, President Emmanuel Macron said on Sunday, after his US counterpart Donald Trump announced a truce along those lines without giving details.

“Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure,” Macron said, adding: “France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky.”

The president of the EU Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has expressed her “full support for President Zelenskyy” amid calls for a ceasefire.

In a telephone call with the Ukrainian leader, von der Leyen posted on X that she “fully supported the call of President Zelenskyy for a ceasefire that would protect global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia.

“The war has entered a new, grimmer phase”, von der Leyen said. “Russia is stalling on the battlefield and striking civilians far behind the front lines.

“I conveyed our solidarity with the Ukrainian people. And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom.”

Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has discussed an energy ceasefire with the leaders of Canada, Finland and Nato and is awaiting details from the US.

Writing on X shortly after saying such a deal was “news to me”, the Ukrainian leader said:

double quotation mark“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it’s important for Russia to support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. From our Ukrainian side, there is always FULL support for de-escalation steps, protection of lives, and the necessary decisions to end the war and ensure lasting peace.”

Russia has yet to comment on Donald Trump’s claim that Kyiv and Moscow had reached an energy ceasefire.

On Friday, Trump had warm words for the Russian president after the country struck a deal to sell diesel fuel to the US in return for sanctions relief.

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Trump said: “That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country. And I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you. We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want, so: thank you.”

A senior Ukrainian official has also reportedly told the FT that Ukraine had no information about Trump’s proclaimed ceasefire deal.

The official was quoted as saying: “Just now our repair teams are restoring electricity and water supplies in Kyiv” following Russian strikes. “Nobody has heard [of the ceasefire].”

Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to make way for a new Ukrainian leader drew criticism from his own party.

Don Bacon, a Republican Nebraska congressman and former military officer, suggested Trump was not fit to lead.

Reacting to Trump’s statement that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’”, Bacon wrote on: “We need a president who is up to the task of leading the free world.”

The latest acrimonious row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukraine’s society to chose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to bow down to US demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” sixty-day ceasefire.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy ⁠has said the “energy ceasefire” was news to him.

He told the news outlet ⁠Axios ​that he was not aware of ⁠an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia announced by ​ ‌Donald Trump, but ‌added that if Moscow ‌agreed to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.

“The ceasefire announcement was news for ‌me. But if Russians agree to an energy ​ceasefire Ukraine will agree. If president Trump negotiated it with ⁠Putin — please tell us ​when ​the ceasefire begins — we ​are ready and ​we ‌will ​accept ​it,” Zelenskiy was quoted as saying by Axios.

In his Truth Social post, Trump gave no further details. The US president had made a similar claim in September, which turned out to be untrue.

Ukraine’s government did not immediately comment on the US president’s latest statement, or confirm a deal had taken place.

Just hours before Donald Trump claimed the two sides had agreed a ceasefire on energy strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rebuffed his demand that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy demanded Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on Ukraine and its energy infrastructure.

Ukraine’s president said any deal to end his country’s long-range drone strikes on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.

Donald Trump has claimed Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an ”energy ceasefire”, though the US president gave no details of the purported agreement.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social account shortly after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told ABC on Sunday that Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire, including on energy infrastructure.

This announcement follows Trump’s criticism of Zelenskyy for attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which he blames for global shortages.

Stick with us as we bring you the latest developments as we get them.

title: Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict
excerpt: Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial r...
body_text:
Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.

Second half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki on Sunday extended City’s flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent -off for two yellow cards.

Victory reestablishes City’s three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against widespread financial impropriety.

An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018.

No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table unless City overturns the decision.

There has even been speculation that there could be retrospective action to strip City’s titles.

The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies.

City’s rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season.

Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years.

“There are so many moments and memories we can’t get back,” Liverpool fan Martin Reilly, 23, told the AFP news agency. “They have to throw the book at them.”

City arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted with bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018.

Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the visitors with chants of “cheats” and “going down”, while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking City’s financial scandal.

In the iconic Kop end behind one goal, a banner read “a generation of supporters cheated”.

The battles between Guardiola’s City and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League’s marquee event.

But with the eyes of the world watching today, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field.

New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola’s options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds.

The home side briefly flickered into life at the start of the second half when Lewis Koumas was denied a goal on his first Premier League start by Gianluigi Donnarumma.

The Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game.

City’s economic might was on full display to help turn the game, as Maresca could turn to Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half.

Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a second yellow card and Liverpool never recovered.

Doku’s deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time and open the floodgates.

Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself.

Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool’s wounds.

City midfielder Elliot Anderson told reporters after the game that his side had shown “courage” as they got the win in a hostile atmosphere.

“We have shown togetherness and fight, this is tough place to come and we have shown courage,” he said.

“It [the noise from the Anfield crowd] was more than normal … Arriving and the first 10 minutes of the first half, but we quietened the crowd and improved in the second half.

“During the game you can feel it, and it is a game where you have to stick together and we did.”

Donald Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action"

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.

The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.

The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and is a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Coordinator told local media.

"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.

The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.

Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023 after previously holding the office from 2007 to 2014.

He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

title: Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial
excerpt:
Democratic Senate candidate’s remarks come as Trump has long baselessly claimed his 2020 election loss was stolen

Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections b...
body_text:
Democratic Senate candidate’s remarks come as Trump has long baselessly claimed his 2020 election loss was stolen

Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday.

El-Sayed’s comments on NBC’s Meet the Press came with the Democrats favored to win control of the House of Representatives during the 3 November midterms – and polls show that the party could also win Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and gain a majority there, too.

Meanwhile, Trump has long baselessly maintained that the 2020 presidential election which he lost as an incumbent to Joe Biden was stolen by fraudsters.

He also gave a primetime speech in July in which he made unverified claims about Chinese interference in the election, and he fired members of an independent federal election commission.

When asked later by a rightwing broadcaster whether the president might declare a national security emergency pertaining to elections for the midterms, Trump ignited alarm among some observers by replying: “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?”

The New York Times, meanwhile, reported that Trump had cast doubt on elections on 440 days of his second presidency, which began in early 2025.

As such, on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday, El-Sayed was asked whether Democrats needed to turn out in such numbers in November that the election would be “too big to rig” – as it had recently been put by former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump.

“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.”

The Cook Political Report revised its predictions on Tuesday and declared that “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”.

A recent New York Times and Siena University poll found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas, states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.

The poll showed El-Sayed leading Republican candidate Mike Rogers by five points.

El-Sayed on Sunday’s Meet the Press alluded to how Rogers had also claimed that a 2024 US Senate election which he lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, was stolen from him – after first having conceded the race.

Rogers in November 2025 was reported to have said at events that a single van carrying fraudulent ballots in Detroit cost him the race against Slotkin.

“The guy … I’m running against insinuates that he didn’t actually lose,” El-Sayed said to Kristen Welker. “That’s the guy I’m running against right now.”

title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
excerpt:
Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure

Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire betw...
body_text:
Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure

Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.

In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.

He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website.

Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.

Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.

There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure.

The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office.

The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on ​Russian energy infrastructure.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.

On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.

Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres.

Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.

The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.

He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”

Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”

Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.

Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”.

Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added.

Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said.

Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber
