title: Manchester-based composer creates requiem to honour enslaved Africans
excerpt:
David Önaç uses insurance documents for work funded by Lloyd’s of London after research uncovered its slavery links

A centuries-old insurance document detailing the trafficking of enslaved Africans b...
body_text:
David Önaç uses insurance documents for work funded by Lloyd’s of London after research uncovered its slavery links

A centuries-old insurance document detailing the trafficking of enslaved Africans began with the words: “In the name of God, Amen.”

For Dr Errol Francis, the artistic director and chief executive of the arts and heritage charity Culture&, the contradiction was striking: an invocation of God in a document that treated human beings as cargo.

It gave him an unusual idea: what if the documents that once insured the trafficking of enslaved Africans could instead be used to create a requiem in their memory?

The new work, Atlantic Requiem, by the Manchester-based composer David Önaç, will premiere on Sunday at LSO St Luke’s in London, performed by the London Symphony Orchestra and BBC Singers.

Commissioned by Culture&, the project grew out of research into Lloyd’s of London, the historic insurance market whose members helped insure ships and enslaved Africans during the transatlantic slave trade.

Sponsored by Lloyd’s, the 40-minute, five-movement work brings together Catholic liturgy, historic insurance documents and testimony concerning the killing of an enslaved African woman aboard a ship in 1790.

Its musical language combines contemporary classical composition with jazz, gospel and other traditions that emerged on both sides of the Atlantic.

The performances, taking place during Black History Month, will be conducted by the Grammy award-winning conductor Malcolm J Merriweather.

“This is a really complicated situation in how religion is being used. Religion was used to convert the indigenous people then, the indigenous people often took up religion as part of emancipation,” Francis, who was a member of the steering group overseeing research into Lloyd’s historical involvement in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans, said.

“That was why I thought to myself, ‘Maybe we should write a Requiem Mass, because that would really bring out these contradictions and also use these documents for a different purpose than what they were intended for.’”

When Culture& approached Önaç about Atlantic Requiem, he jumped at the opportunity. “The styles that I’m interested in come from both sides of the Atlantic, so it just felt like I finally had this grand canvas on which I could explore these dual interests, allow the two styles to enrich one another,” he said.

For Önaç, who is of mixed heritage and hails from both sides of the Atlantic, the piece was an opportunity to explore longstanding questions about where he belongs.

“As a pianist, sometimes the piano itself and the layout or the geography is an inspiration to me,” he said.

“When you took the five black notes and two of the significant white notes from the other set, you got this seven-note blues scale, which is the product of the musical and cultural experience of enslaved Africans from the other side of the Atlantic.”

But while the work ultimately moves towards reconciliation and joy, some of its most harrowing passages confront the violence of enslavement directly. The second movement draws on a 1791 grand jury testimony concerning the killing of an enslaved African woman aboard the brig Polly, commanded by James DeWolf.

The testimony, preserved by the Newport Historical Society, records the account of John Cranston, a crew member who described a horrific incident during the ship’s voyage from Africa to the West Indies in 1791.

According to Cranston, an enslaved woman suspected of having smallpox was bound to a chair, gagged and thrown overboard on the captain’s orders, amid fears she would infect others aboard the ship.

“There’s bits in it that I get tearful even just talking about it,” Francis said. “It is about people who’ve passed away, but it’s also about the fact that we have survived this incredible trauma.”

For Önaç, the combination of the words and the music were at times so powerful that it felt overwhelming.

“The captain’s words were that he was sorry because he’d lost such a good chair,” he said. “I felt we needed to hear and see and experience what the human impact is here. What is the emotional impact? What is the loss of culture? What is the blindness to value?”

Lloyd’s has acknowledged its historical links to enslavement, and after the publication of the Underwriting Souls interactive archive, it announced its Inclusive Futures programme, aimed at supporting Black and ethnically diverse communities.

For some, this artistic project doesn’t go far enough. But Francis is careful to distinguish the requiem from important questions of financial redress.

“It’s not about reparations; it’s about an artwork that acknowledges the suffering, but also the survival of African people,” he said.

Önaç added that the requiem is not only a response to historical atrocities but a commentary on modern society.

“Everything’s so polarised and segregated and polemical right now, it seems to me, and I’ve tried to portray that in the black and white notes.

“It’s not just for then; it’s a commentary on now as well.”

title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
excerpt:
Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page

You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google c...
body_text:
Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page

You’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them.

Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank, or another institution.

Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.

The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.

It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.

“Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.”

And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says.

Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software.

“That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.”

If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”.

You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals.

Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says.

Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.”

The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number.

Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.”

Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details.

As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”.

Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link.

“My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.”

Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted.

He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
excerpt:
Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold

New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade...
body_text:
Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold

New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election.

Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week.

The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell, but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come.

The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills, a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000.

Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.”

Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party, though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit.

Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.”

Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England.

The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression.

“Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.”

While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power.

Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation.

Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes.

“With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.”

The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds.

Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.”

At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid, alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades. There was also a nod towards localised support for nature with a community fund for planting 500,000 trees across England.

McCarthy said: “Voters will be comparing Labour with other parties that have a clear plan to lower energy bills and tackle the climate crisis rather than with the fantasies of the Conservatives and Reform. Labour has a clear plan but needs to deliver it – starting with a full-throated rejection of any scramble for fossil fuels in the North Sea.”

The decision on the future of the Rosebank and Jackdaw drilling sites was reportedly postponed for the byelection, and McCarthy said it would “truly define this government’s legacy on climate”.

Failure to recognise and tackle the damage caused to the UK by a summer of record heat and drought would prove costly, campaigners warned. A record El Niño weather system is brewing, super-charged by global heating and likely to bring heatwaves, droughts and floods to key agricultural areas, pushing millions into hunger and raising food prices globally.

Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “With El Niño bringing a wetter and stormier winter season to the UK, we desperately need to see some parties getting back in touch with reality. The government must translate its words into action that delivers for people and the planet.”

title: Vinicius apologises for hair-pull red card but could miss El Clasico
excerpt: Real Madrid’s Vinicius Jr has apologised ⁠⁠to ⁠⁠his teammates and the club’s fans after being sent off in the 1-0 ⁠⁠win over Villarreal in La Liga at the Santiago Bernabeu but now faces a ⁠⁠nervous wa...
body_text:
Real Madrid’s Vinicius Jr has apologised ⁠⁠to ⁠⁠his teammates and the club’s fans after being sent off in the 1-0 ⁠⁠win over Villarreal in La Liga at the Santiago Bernabeu but now faces a ⁠⁠nervous wait for a ruling by the disciplinary committee, which could see him miss Real’s fixture with rivals Barcelona in two weeks.

The Brazilian thought he had scored Real’s second goal in the match on Saturday, but his effort was disallowed after a video assistant referee (VAR) review found he should be dismissed for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair in the build-up.

After the match, Vinicius, ⁠⁠who came on in the ⁠⁠52nd minute and was red-carded 20 minutes later, posted on social media, saying, “sorry to the team and the ⁠⁠fans”.

Vinicius was celebrating after scoring when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera was called by the VAR to review the moments before his goal. The referee waved off the goal and pulled out a red card for Vinicius.

When he thought Vinicius had doubled the lead, Real manager Jose Mourinho ran to join the celebrations with his players.

But moments later, Vinicius was left livid by the referee’s decision. He screamed at Diaz de Mera while his teammates tried to calm him down as he left the field.

“I don’t think he meant to hurt anyone, but it is a red card,” Villarreal defender Juan Foyth said about the hair yank of Saliba.

Diaz de Mera wrote in his match report that after being shown the red card, Vinicius “protested my decision, raising his voice, toward where I was standing in an aggressive manner, and being held back by teammates”.

Royal Spanish Football Federation regulations state that pulling an opponent’s hair ⁠⁠is regarded as violent conduct.

The ⁠⁠sanction for violent conduct without causing injury to an opponent, according to Article 130 of the league’s rules, is a ban of one to three ‌‌matches.

Real’s next three La Liga games are against Sevilla, Barca and Racing Santander, but missing El ‌‌Clasico ‌‌would be a bitter blow for the 26-year-old Brazil international.

Mourinho did not appear at the mandatory post-game news conference.

title: Delaware neighborhood on edge after masked men with apparent weapons knock on doors of homes
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Cameras in a Delaware neighborhood caught at least two masked men knocking on doors late Friday night, including one c...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Cameras in a Delaware neighborhood caught at least two masked men knocking on doors late Friday night, including one carrying an apparent rifle, police said.

Images released by the New Castle County Police Department show a man wearing a tactical-style vest and holding what appears to be a rifle while knocking on a home's front door.

A separate image shows another individual approaching a front door wearing a black vest and mask.

TIMELINE REVEALS HOW MAN IN 'CHUCKY' MASK TERRORIZED PHILADELPHIA STREETS, EVADED POLICE

New Castle County police are investigating reports of masked individuals knocking on residents' doors while allegedly carrying what appeared to be weapons. (New Castle County Police)

According to police, officers were called to the 1200 block of Canvasback Drive in Mallard Pointe, New Castle, around 10:50 p.m. Friday following a report of a suspicious person.

Residents told police that a man wearing a black hockey-style mask and tactical-style vest approached homes while carrying what appeared to be a rifle.

MAN WITH JOKER-INSPIRED RIFLE FIRES GUN, RUNS INTO TRAFFIC NEAR TRUMP GOLF COURSE, DEPUTIES SAY

A masked individual wearing a tactical-style vest and carrying what appeared to be a rifle was captured on camera approaching a home in New Castle, Delaware, on Oct. 9, 2026, according to police. (New Castle County Police)

The man allegedly knocked on doors before running away, according to police.

Authorities said four men were also seen heading eastbound on Mallard Road — two on bicycles and two on foot.

Officers and a K-9 unit conducted a search of the neighborhood and nearby properties but could not locate the individuals.

Although police have not confirmed whether the weapons were real firearms, they said they believe the weapons may have been airsoft-style guns.

A second individual wearing a black vest and mask was photographed approaching a home's front door in the Mallard Pointe neighborhood of New Castle, Delaware. (New Castle County Police)

Anyone with information about the incident or home security footage from the surrounding area is urged to call 911 or the department's non-emergency number at 302-573-2800.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
excerpt:
As Israel entered the final month before its October 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a chilling warning to share.

Israel’s enemies, he said on September 29, were plotting an attack...
body_text:
As Israel entered the final month before its October 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a chilling warning to share.

Israel’s enemies, he said on September 29, were plotting an attack on the country before the vote. Without providing any evidence, he then quickly referred to continuing attacks by Israeli troops in the Gaza Strip, where he said they had killed more than 100 “terrorists” in recent weeks.

That link drawn by Netanyahu – between the genocidal war on Gaza that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, the upcoming elections, and Israel’s national security – was not coincidental, say analysts.

Netanyahu’s insistence that he alone can secure Israelis from a range of threats they face from across the country’s borders, they say, lies at the heart of his re-election campaign, even as his alleged failures during the attack three years ago and in securing the quick release of captives have offered his opponents ammunition.

When a Flydubai flight packed with Israeli passengers on their way from Dubai to Tel Aviv a day after his recent warning nearly crashed after a co-pilot attacked his pilot with an axe in the cockpit, Netanyahu was quick to seize on the incident to argue that he is still man for the country’s top job.

Polls suggest that he faces a stiff test in what is the first general vote since the 2023 attacks, which led to the killing of 1,139 people in Israel and triggered the genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where Israeli have attacks have since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.

Three years later, the war has become inseparable from the domestic debate over Israel’s direction while also accelerating a political shift to the right – with once-fringe positions on Palestinians now very much the mainstream view.

Few embody this transformation more than Israel’s far-right financial Minister Bezalel Smotrich, sanctioned by a number of Western countries and known for his incendiary and racist language and policies towards Palestinians.

In one of his characteristically inflammatory statements, Smotrich told Israeli outlet Ynet late last month that the Israeli army should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”.

Less than two weeks later, Smotrich’s electoral ally Moshe Feiglin added fuel to the fire.

“The enemy is Gaza, not Hamas”, he told the Jerusalem Post, calling for the annexation of the besieged territory after the election. “The baby that will be born tomorrow in Gaza will do exactly the same,” he said, in reference to the 2023 attacks.

Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar said these are not “stray comments” from marginal figures but an electoral message from power-seeking politicians aimed at portraying Palestinians as “not a people with rights, but a demographic and security problem to be expelled, conquered or destroyed”.

He added: “The frightening reality is that the coming election risks becoming a competition not over whether Palestinian life should be protected, but over who can promise to erase it most aggressively.”

Following October 7, the younger generation in particular slid rightwards, said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.

He said the forces driving Israel to the right had been gathering for decades.

“The trend toward the right began after the Yom Kippur War in 1973, but it has intensified dramatically since October 7,” Bregman told Al Jazeera, referring to the bloody 19-day October War, or the 1973 Arab-Israeli War – a conflict between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria.

More recently, the far right has been emboldened through electoral politics as part of Netanyahu’s government since 2022 – the most right-wing government in Israeli history.

Another outspoken cabinet member alongside Smotrich is Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right provocateur who has previously been convicted of inciting racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation.

“Netanyahu’s greatest mistake – among many – was bringing figures like Ben-Gvir and Smotrich into his coalition,” said Bergman. “By doing so, he legitimised them as influential forces in Israeli politics.”

Ben-Gvir has been so cemented into Israel’s political system, he has hopes pinned on becoming the next Israeli defence minister, the analyst pointed out.

“This is madness. But that’s contemporary Israel,” said Bergman.

Analysts also pointed out that several parties running, including ones that are currently in power and a number that are challenging the current coalition, all advocate for the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza, as one of the examples of the shift to the right.

Omar Baddar, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, said the messaging from across the Israeli political and military spectrum in the lead-up to the election shows that there is “a consensus” to continue the attacks on Gaza, where nearly 1,500 have been killed since a “ceasefire” last year.

“They’re using the threats to get more votes,” he said, pointing out to what he described as the radicalisation of the society.

With the election approaching, added Baddar, Israeli leaders are seeking to undo one another: “Who[ever]’s more radical is more likely to get more votes.”

As Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher from inside Israel, writes, “what it means to be ‘right-wing’ in Israel today is above all to take a harder line on Palestinian national claims, security and territorial control.”

He adds: “On security and the Palestinians, a large part of Jewish Israeli politics already works from assumptions that would have been treated as right-wing a generation ago: Deep suspicion of a sovereign Palestinian state, a high tolerance for prolonged military control, and a stronger insistence on Jewish sovereignty as the starting point rather than one value among others.”

Observers and rights groups say the disparity is even evident in the electoral process. A prominent politician and Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, has been forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their violent rhetoric against Palestinians.

Recent polling indicates that the events of October 7 are top of mind for Israelis, who also have questions about who was responsible for the security failures of that day.

Just last month, reports surfaced indicating that Netanyahu had received two separate warnings about an imminent Hamas attack in 2023, from Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, and United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have cited the alleged warnings to call the prime minister “unfit” to remain at the helm of the country.

But Netanyahu has denied suggestions that he had been forewarned about the attack, and the reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on opinion polls.

While October 7 represents a profound rupture in Israelis’ sense of security, public trust in the Netanyahu government had already been badly shaken by its controversial judicial overhaul, introduced when the prime minister’s current coalition first came to power, said Mairav Zonszein, an Israel-Palestine analyst at the International Crisis Group based in Tel Aviv.

Despite these breaches of trust, the Israeli leader retains support.

“Israelis in general still see Netanyahu as kind of the guy on security. And more to the point, they don’t really see an alternative,” Zonszein told Al Jazeera.

A June survey by Mitvim – the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies found that the Israeli public supports its government’s military and security solutions, and rejects resolving the Palestinian issue and ending the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory. This is the case even while it has been concerned about international isolation and the decline of Israel’s international standing since the beginning of the genocidal war on Gaza, the survey reported.

Yet Israelis are also increasingly war-weary, even as they back the use of more force. Its troops – stretched between six fronts of war in the last few years – are bearing the brunt of this fatigue in Israeli society.

Israel’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday that nearly 30,000 soldiers and security personnel are facing psychological trauma since the war.

The ministry said its rehabilitation department’s budget has increased by 88 percent over the past three years to 10 billion shekels ($3.3m), with the majority supporting treatment for mental health conditions and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Still, Israel in recent months has been more and more vocal about its expansionist vision, with officials brazenly stating the goal of “Greater Israel”. The claim for the conquest is based on a biblical verse (Genesis 15:18-21).

For decades, Israel has ignored international law in its continuous occupation of Palestinian and Syrian land, and has shown little respect for its neighbours’ sovereignty, occupying more land in Syria, as well as in Lebanon in more recent years.

According to Najar, the political economist, the “complete dehumanisation” of Palestinians as evidenced during the campaign reveal that Gaza “is being presented to Israeli voters not as a catastrophe or a crime for which there must be accountability, but as a blueprint to be repeated elsewhere”.

In southern Lebanon, where Israel has been carrying out near daily attacks and and has occupied large swathes of land, residents have told Al Jazeera they expect little to change even if Netanyahu is defeated in the election.

Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot – head of the Yashar party and former army chief of staff – is the father of the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, and is just as hawkish about expansion. That doctrine, since Israel’s war with the Lebanese group Hezbollah in 2006, calls for the use of huge force, even against civilian infrastructure, as a deterrent against enemies and was deployed in Israel’s recent wars, particularly in Beirut’s southern suburbs.

If it were up to Eisenkot, the Lebanon front of war would have never scaled down: He has accused Netanyahu of bowing to US pressure to halt operations in Beirut, and has insisted that the military should be able to attack Hezbollah anywhere in Lebanon.

For Israelis still reeling from the events of October 7, Eisenkot could fill the security void many are feeling, said Zonszein.

“They really … see the world as kind of very hostile towards them, the world not understanding what they went through on October 7, and [therefore why] the need to have these security buffer zones in Lebanon, in Syria, and Gaza,” she said.

A two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is therefore out of the question, said the analysts – and has not even made a blip of an appearance in campaigning before the election.

The idea first emerged during the Oslo Accords more than 30 years ago, which set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, predicated on the belief that the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel was imperative to forge peace.

But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state.

“The concept of a two-state solution is currently irrelevant and likely will remain so for another decade or two, if not longer,” said Bergman. “It is unlikely to become a reality in the foreseeable future, as no Israeli leader can propose it to the Israeli public after the events of October 7.”

The only way it could regain prominence is if there is substantial international pressure, including severe sanctions on Israel, and a non-violent intifada, or an uprising by Palestinians, he said.

The outright rejection of Palestinian statehood has simply become much more “acceptable”, said Zonszein.

“There’s several parties who advocate these views, whereas there isn’t a single Jewish Zionist Party that puts the need for a two-state solution or a Palestinian political process at the forefront,” she said.

Taken all together, Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.

“[There’s] more and more movement towards more military force, more need for pushing the borders … out of a lot of fear that another October 7 could happen,” said Zonszein.

title: Ben Roberts-Smith attends Canberra event honouring Australian troops who served in Afghanistan
excerpt:
Anthony Albanese speaks at Australian War Memorial event commemorating 25th anniversary of country’s involvement in the conflict

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony A...
body_text:
Anthony Albanese speaks at Australian War Memorial event commemorating 25th anniversary of country’s involvement in the conflict

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese has honoured Australian troops who served in Afghanistan, using the 25th anniversary of the country’s involvement in the conflict to describe their heroism as a fight for “who we are as a people”.

The prime minister joined hundreds of veterans, family members and dignitaries at a commemoration of the start of the campaign in Canberra on Sunday, with nation’s most decorated living soldier and accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith among the crowd at the Australian War Memorial.

“In New York, fires were still burning at Ground Zero from the September 11 attacks a month earlier. The world felt upended,” Albanese said of the start of Operation Slipper.

“Though it would change so devastatingly a year later in Bali, it was not yet directly our fight.

“Yet Australia did what is so resolutely in our nature. We went to support our friend and ally.

“We went because we saw what was at stake, and we went on the principle that September 11 was an attack on a way of life that belonged just as much to us.”

He said the more than 35,000 defence force members deployed over the following two decades did so because the very freedoms “that are at the heart of who we are as a people and a nation were under threat”.

Roberts-Smith, who denies the allegations against him, attended the event alongside family members and supporters, as well as former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison.

The governor general, Sam Mostyn, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, were also present in the bright sunshine.

Roberts-Smith was awarded Australia’s highest military honour – the Victoria Cross – for his service in Afghanistan, but now faces accusations he murdered five unarmed detainees during his deployment.

The former Special Air Service regiment corporal sat alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin, after a judge agreed to vary his bail conditions to allow him to visit Canberra.

Deployments to the Middle East continued until withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021.

US troops left a few months later after signing an agreement with the Taliban, who swiftly returned to power and reintroduced authoritarian control, including strict suppression of women and girls’ rights.

Some 47 Australian personnel died as a result of their service and 263 were wounded, while thousands more allied soldiers were killed.

Tens of thousands of civilians were also estimated to have been killed during the war.

Despite the controversy over Australia’s military involvement in Afghanistan and its legacy, the troops who served on the ground remain intensely proud of what they achieved.

Soldier Mathew Bell was deployed in 2012, aged 24, with his infantry battalion to a forward operating base in Afghanistan’s “badlands” west of Tarinkot.

More than a decade after he returned to Australia, Bell remembers his unit’s work with a sense of honour and accomplishment.

“We changed that little part of Afghanistan, that little part of the world for good,” the former lance corporal, now 38, said.

Bell said girls were able to attend school, medical services were rolled out to villages and “there was freedom”.

“Not the oppression we’re seeing now under the Taliban government,” the father of two said.

“Our role was essentially to go out on either vehicle-mounted patrols or foot patrols, out among the local population through the desert, through the green zone, keeping the Taliban at bay.

“It was a hot area. Once you stepped over that line in the sand, like, that was Taliban territory.”

One of Bell’s close mates was badly wounded in a roadside bomb explosion and on more than one occasion, his section was pinned down by sniper fire.

Services were also held at the Anzac Memorial in Sydney’s Hyde Park, at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance and other sites around the country.

Australians who served in the Afghanistan War were deployed in various roles and missions contributing to reconstruction efforts, democratic governance, training and humanitarian aid.

Operation Slipper was followed between 2015 and 2021 by Operation Highroad and the Kabul airlift in August 2021.

title: Two Carlton players treated in hospital after off-season night out
excerpt:
Club issues brief statement about Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, saying latter suffered minor cut to head after a fall

An off-season night out for Carlton football club teammates ended with two playe...
body_text:
Club issues brief statement about Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, saying latter suffered minor cut to head after a fall

An off-season night out for Carlton football club teammates ended with two players admitted to hospital for treatment on Sunday morning, in what the club says are “separate circumstances”.

The club released a statement on Sunday confirming that players Lachie Cowan, 21, and Will Hayward, 27, had been treated and discharged, after reports in several media outlets about the aftermath of an off-season night out.
 Guardian Australia understands both players were both part of a larger group that had been socialising on Saturday evening.

The club statement said Cowan had “received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later” but did not provide any more information about the circumstances.

Hayward was also admitted to hospital later on Sunday morning, after returning home.

“Will Hayward experienced a minor cut to the head after a fall, and admitted himself to hospital where he received stitches before being discharged,” Carlton said.

Neither player is understood to be seriously unwell or hurt.

“The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances.”

Ambulance Victoria said paramedics responded to an incident at inner-suburban South Yarra at about 5.15am on Sunday.

A man in his 20s was taken by ambulance to the Alfred hospital in stable condition, Ambulance Victoria said.

Players throughout the league are on leave as trade period rolls on until Wednesday night.

title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
excerpt:
The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month

The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal...
body_text:
The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month

The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.

Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.

The justice department asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said that the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.

Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.

A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ​news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

The television networks have not yet commented.

Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.

The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban

Major US outlets suspend shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban

title: ‘Restore the authority’: the challenge for the BBC’s new director of news
excerpt:
Rachel Jupp takes role as corporation grapples with digital transformation, a cash crisis and its public service role

With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been much to smil...
body_text:
Rachel Jupp takes role as corporation grapples with digital transformation, a cash crisis and its public service role

With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been much to smile about for BBC journalists working in “the pit” – their pet name for the newsroom deep in the belly of New Broadcasting House.

On Monday afternoon, however, they were greeted by a grinning figure conducting a tour of the news floor. She was Rachel Jupp, the BBC’s newly appointed director of news and current affairs. Jupp engaged in a series of polite if brief conversations with her new troops.

It was a small but welcome gesture for a newsroom that had been desperate for a sense of direction from a new, permanent leader. The shock resignation of Deborah Turness, Jupp’s predecessor, was almost a year ago. Frustration has grown among journalists awaiting a grand plan.

“We just need a set direction of travel,” said one. “A north star, as startups call it. Lay out a timeline and tell everyone what cuts are coming and what needs to be done.”

Beyond the small talk, figures at all levels of the corporation acknowledge that Jupp faces a huge task. Running the world’s most scrutinised newsroom is a tall order at the best of times, even without the turmoil over pay and job losses.

Jupp takes the helm at BBC News as it is gripped by an angst-ridden debate about the place of its journalism in an increasingly digital world. It is one she has been tasked with resolving.

It is a world in which the BBC’s hallmarks of impartiality and authority – and focus on television and radio news – are pitted against content creators and a myriad of other established media brands converging to reach audiences via a handful of smartphone apps.

Inside BBC News, a series of announcements about show closures and strategy shifts have fuelled a “clicks v public service” debate. There are competing views over how the BBC should adapt its content for commercially driven digital platforms favoured by younger audiences – while sticking to the corporation’s founding principles of informing the public.

“I’ve heard the DG [director general, Matt Brittin] and [the deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies] have been saying to people that they want the new director of news to restore the authority of BBC News,” said Roger Mosey, the former head of BBC TV News.

“I think that’s what a lot of us have been arguing for. BBC News does all sorts of good things and it’s generally an impartial and fair service. But it hasn’t been able to translate the authority of the really big brands of TV and radio into an online world.”

Those concerned that the corporation is at risk of losing its bearings point to a BBC website piece about penis fillers or recent social videos of reporters holding cheap mics, content creator-style. Meanwhile, they fear flagship shows such as the Today programme or the 10 O’Clock News, which continue to attract large audiences, have not been nourished or championed online.

Those pushing for a faster embrace of new platforms say it is clearly where audiences are heading and the broadcaster’s requirement to cater for everyone is at the heart of its public service remit. As one BBC figure put it: “Rachel’s task and challenge is to show how we can do what every news organisation is having to do – go digital, without becoming a value-free click factory.”

Above all else, Jupp’s willingness to take on this precarious task is why she was handed such a big promotion.

While the BBC’s relatively new director general, Matt Brittin, inherited many of the cuts being announced across the BBC, Jupp’s appointment was in his hands. At an all-staff call this week, he said he wanted the organisation to be “a bit more Elvis – a little less conversation, a little more action”. In Jupp, Brittin believes he has found one of his best Elvis impersonators, willing to make changes for the digital age.

Jupp triumphed from a shortlist of four candidates. There was a recognition that one of her competitors, Jonathan Munro, had managed to avoid any major crises as the interim head of BBC News – an achievement not to be underestimated, given recent criticisms.

However, the job came down to Jupp and Esme Wren, the editor of Channel 4 News. Wren was recognised as a formidable champion of journalists and journalism, but the conclusion was that the BBC’s news machine produces plenty of high-quality, award-winning material.

While Jupp had not run a big organisation before – something Brittin had been looking for – the director general believed Jupp had two important qualities. The first was solid editorial judgment – a requirement after bruising criticisms over a Gaza documentary that had to be pulled and a spliced-together Trump speech that led to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit.

Jupp had been tasked with overseeing the BBC’s documentary and long-form journalism content after the Gaza row, so was seen as someone who would safeguard the BBC’s authority as it pushed deeper into digital content.

Her second quality was an appetite for transformation, the buzzword for the mammoth task of translating the BBC’s journalism on to new digital platforms without losing its authority – seen, at best, as a work in progress. Jupp has also been at the heart of the BBC’s use of generative AI, and Brittin – a former Google executive – believes this can have a bigger role if used in the right way.

It also helped that Jupp could start almost immediately, given the pace at which a cash crisis is forcing the BBC into big, strategic choices.

Jupp also begins her tenure with another underrated advantage: she is genuinely liked by close colleagues and respected by journalists who have worked with her in previous roles at Channel 4 News, Newsnight and Panorama.

As her tour of the pit illustrated, starting with the support of her staff is seen as essential as she embarks on a transformation of BBC News that will include some difficult and unpopular decisions.

title: Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader
excerpt:
NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers

Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving...
body_text:
NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers

Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had a devastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.

Speaking to the Guardian, Kebede called on the government to roll out a mass retrofitting programme to ensure schools – which he said had been built “for a different climate” – were better equipped to deal with extreme heat ahead of next summer’s El Niño-charged temperatures.

And he said it was time for a national conversation about other measures that could help schools adapt to the reality of a rapidly warming climate.

“There needs to be a really serious discussion about how we make sure there is the continuity of education in this changed climate,” he said. “You might want to consider moving the school year around, or having a longer summer holiday – in hot countries they tend to have a longer summer holiday. You might consider an earlier start and earlier finish … and perhaps we don’t want exams to be happening in the hottest part of the year.”

Kebede said he had been inundated with messages from teachers during this summer’s heatwaves urging the union to help.

“The last time I felt that level of panic in the profession was during the Covid pandemic,” he said. “I was being routinely contacted by members in distress … they felt there was a real risk and danger to themselves and to their pupils.”

At least 760,000 schoolchildren in England and Wales missed lessons owing to school closures during this summer’s June heatwave – one in five in the UK in the space of a few months – with pupils missing more than 15m hours of lesson time.

School staff told the Guardian that learning was almost impossible as temperature records were broken, with pupil behaviour and attention deteriorating rapidly.

One primary school teacher said: “Everyone was lying or sitting on the floor with their water bottles, sweating, moaning and feeling tired, [complaining of] headaches and nausea. The adults barely coped and most of the children were calling for their mummies and daddies. There was no learning, just surviving the best we could.”

This summer’s severe heat was not confined to the UK: brutal temperatures and devastating wildfires hit countries across Europe. One of the key demands of the student protesters that have taken to the streets in France this week has been action to make classrooms bearable during extreme heat.

Kebede warned that in the UK the impact of these bouts of extreme weather was falling hardest on more disadvantaged communities. He said children were often being sent home to flats that were unsuited to extreme heat, and to parents and carers who were unable to work from home or take time off.

“It is having a really uneven impact and it’s particularly impacting children who live in deprived urban areas … you will have a two-tier system where schools in more affluent areas are able to cope with extreme heat.”

Kebede said many of the UK’s schools were housed in either old Victorian-era buildings or those built in the 1960s and 1970s, and neither style was equipped to cope with the extreme heat that is expected to become a feature of UK summers.

He said a major capital building programme could transform schools, making them “fit for the century we are living in” and also creating good unionised apprenticeships and jobs, revitalising local communities.

“We really need plans in place now because [what we experienced this summer] is going to be the norm,” Kebede said.

title: Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?
excerpt:
Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight

It took more than an hour to establish the two intra...
body_text:
Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight

It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.

“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”

When the team finally achieved what they thought would be a working line, allowing her execution to proceed, Pike, 50, made a point of thanking them. “Miss Pike was kind, and she was cooperative,” her lawyer Randy Spivey, a witness in the death chamber, said.

The world knows what happened next. For reasons as yet not fully understood, the drug did not enter her bloodstream, probably spilling into her arm tissue.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder when she was 18 of her classmate Colleen Slemmer, remained alive. She is the only person ever to survive a full “lethal” injection execution.

On Tuesday she remarkably regained consciousness. She is now able to talk and walk around the room, her lawyers have said.

In comments to reporters, Spivey said that he was haunted by the harrowing failed execution. “What I saw is not something that should ever happen again. It was done in all of our names.”

The events of the past 10 days – starting with Pike amicably assisting her executioners and ending with her waking up shackled to a Nashville hospital bed, her arms grotesquely swollen, facing a long and uncertain road to recovery – has thrown America into a frenzy. If this is the outcome of a punishment carried out in “all our names”, then what are we doing about it?

“This is a very big moment,” said Laura Porter, executive director at the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, an alliance of 60 abolitionist groups. “When you see something as horrific as this, the impact is enormous, as it throws attention on the death penalty’s flaws.”

Porter has been closely involved in America’s struggle with capital punishment for almost a quarter century, since she became a leader of New Yorkers Against the Death Penalty in 2003. At that time death row prisoners were still being killed at a rate of more than one a week.

There were 71 executions that year in the US (down from the 1999 pinnacle of 98). Since then, Porter has watched and agitated as the number has steadily declined for almost two decades, reaching a low of just 11 judicial killings in 2021.

“I believe that the death penalty will die by a thousand cuts,” she said. “Every time there’s a botched execution like Christa’s, or a wrongful conviction, or the execution of an intellectually disabled person, public understanding of the system’s flaws grows.”

How great a difference a few years can make. Six years ago, there was such confidence in the historic fading away of the practice that the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) began its yearly report with the words: “Capital punishment continued to wither across the US in 2019”.

But as Mark Twain might have put it, reports of the death penalty’s own death turned out to be an exaggeration. Fast forward to last year, and DPI was recording that the 47 executions carried out in 2025 marked the highest incidence in 16 years.

No awards for guessing the key individual behind the resurgence. Less than a year after DPI’s “withering” pronouncement, Donald Trump embarked on one of the most concentrated bursts of US state killing of its own citizens in modern times.

Toward the end of his first presidency, the Trump administration executed 13 federal death row prisoners. They included Lisa Montgomery, a woman with such a shocking history of childhood sexual abuse it bears comparison to Pike’s own.

Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions. On his first day back he issued an executive order on “restoring the death penalty” in which he said it was “an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes”.

The statement was a classic Trump fabrication. The US justice department itself has concluded that there is no proof that the punishment deters criminals. Many prisoners on death row cannot be described as the most heinous, not least the 4% who by conservative estimations are innocent.

At federal level, Trump has been hampered by Joe Biden, who before he left office commuted the death penalties of all but three prisoners on federal death row. Using his power as commander-in-chef, Trump still managed this week to order the military execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooter.

On Thursday the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, breathlessly announced that Hasan would face a firing squad of soldiers at Fort Hood on 3 December in the first public execution to be staged in the US since 1936. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

The Pentagon’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution prompted a second wave of desbelief that ricocheted around the globe , threatening to drown out even the consternation over Pike’s treatment. US politicians denounced the idea as “disgusting”, while the UN issued the US government with the same stern warning it has given Afghanistan and Iran that the move would be tantamount to torture.

When not presiding over an administration that seems determined to turn the clock back 100 years, Trump has also used his squawk box to exhort death penalty states, where most capital punishment activity occurs, to hit the gas. Many have obliged.

First among them has been Florida. The outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, appears to have been so inspired by Trump’s 2020-21 killing spree that he greenlit a record 19 executions last year.

DeSantis will come close to matching that shattering number in 2026. Florida has already put to death 16 prisoners this year, with two more executions pending, though the governor cancelled a lethal injection procedure on Friday without giving an explanation.

Nationwide, the US is set to kill up to 38 people this year – the most recent just on Wednesday when Texas executed convicted murderer Jamaal Howard. That tally would be down from last year’s high, but still represent a larger display of state killing than in any year since 2013.

In cheerleading the revival of executions, Trump has been backed by a supporting cast of Christian nationalists. These Bible thumpers have injected their eye-for-an-eye brand of retributive justice into the wider Maga movement.

Brooklyn Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, has studied Christian nationalist views on justice. She has found them to be far more embracing of retribution, including the death sentence, than other US religious groups.

Christian nationalist leaders frequently invoke Old Testament notions of punitive justice “as part of the idea of creating a social order, and then requiring people to fit within it,” Walker said.

Doug Wilson, an Idaho pastor who wants to turn America into a theocracy and has close ties to Hegseth, has pushed for legal appeals to be streamlined. That way death row prisoners could be dispatched more quickly.

Joel Webbon, another leading Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, has argued for the death penalty to be expanded to include women who make false sexual assault accusations. The day after Pike’s failed execution he posted to his 120,000 followers on X that “you cannot be pro life without being pro death penalty”.

The energy blown into capital punishment from such far-right religious pundits is affecting the furious debate that has now erupted in Tennessee over what should happen to Pike. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for Tennessee governor, wants to plug back in the electric chair.

Blackburn’s call for the return of “Old Sparky” speaks volumes about the state of capital punishment. The horrifying scenes at Pike’s attempted execution were part of a wider unravelling of lethal injections, the protocol that has been dominant in the US for almost 50 years.

By DPI’s calculations, there have been 12 botched executions in the past five years alone. Five of the condemned prisoners involved, including Pike herself, survived the procedure meaning that they were rendered immobile while a team of masked strangers failed to kill them for up to several hours.

Amid such unconscionable suffering, the claim made on behalf of lethal injections that they are a medicalised and humane form of ending a life has come unstuck. Who would dare to classify what Pike endured as humane?

Proponents of the ultimate punishment have been forced to seek alternatives that might avoid some of the pitfalls of lethal injections. But the moment they have introduced such often archaic methods they have run into a whole new set of headaches.

Two of the prisoners who survived recent lethal injections, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, were executed by Alabama a year later under the experimental technique, nitrogen gas. The method is regarded by veterinarians as too cruel for the euthanisia of cats and dogs, and it has now been blocked for human use by a federal court.

Other states have tried the firing squad. But when South Carolina took this path last year with Mikal Mahdi, a convicted murderer, the marksmen missed the target of the prisoner’s heart, causing him a prolonged and likely agonising death.

Such an avalanche of mishaps, spanning botched executions, experimentation, and even dark insinuations of deliberate miss-targeting, is what Porter means by her “death by a thousand cuts”. It gives her and her army of abolitionists the material they need to sustain a long campaign.

As a seasoned abolitionist, Porter knows that she is facing tough adversaries in Trump and the Christian nationalists. But she draws sustenance from the 23 states that have scrapped the death penalty which, if you add the four states that have put the practice on hold, pushes them into the majority.

Then there is the growing number of young Americans who no longer support the punishment. In the most recent Gallup poll that asked the question, from 2024, only 42% of 18 to 34 year olds approved. (In last year’s poll the overall extent of support had fallen from a 1995 high of 80% to 52%).

She also takes heart from the burgeoning ranks of Republican state lawmakers willing to raise objections. And by the increasing unwillingness of juries to mete out new death sentences.

Most of all, she’s buoyed up by the powerful accord she has found from an unlikely source: families of capital murder victims. Amid their grief, some families have had the strength and conviction to join the fight to spare the lives of those who killed their loved ones.

“In every campaign I’ve been part of where we’ve ended the death penalty – in Connecticut, Maryland, Virginia, and many more – victims’ families have been among the lead voices,” Porter said.

To those voices we may perhaps, in time, be able to add one more. It would be the most unlikely voice of all – that of a woman whom the modern state, with all its paraphernalia, could not silence: Christa Pike.

Her lawyers tell us that she is angry and confused, her mind foggy. But she is also able to inquire after the well-being of others, including, poignantly, the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer.

She is not out of the woods: on Saturday she was released from hospital and returned to the women’s prison in Nashville, where she will still receive medical care. But coming from a state of unconsciousness so profound that even her own legal team feared she might be brain-dead, her reemergence has been nothing short of astonishing.

It all leaves so many questions, her lawyer Spivey said ruefully on Wednesday. “We have to ask, ‘How much suffering is enough?’”

Spivey directed the question at Tennessee. He might just as well have been addressing America.

title: US opens antitrust probe into TV networks for halting Trump coverage
excerpt:
The United States Department of Justice has opened an investigation into television networks’ decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month.

A spokesperson said on Saturday that the ...
body_text:
The United States Department of Justice has opened an investigation into television networks’ decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month.

A spokesperson said on Saturday that the department was investigating whether the networks violated federal antitrust laws by their boycott, which followed a White House decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations, including CNN.

The ⁠networks under investigation are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, said Emily Convington, the Justice Department spokesperson.

“Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” she said of the antitrust legislation.

“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

The investigation is the latest in a series ‌of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations. Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media “fake news” and frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press.

The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.

The networks did not immediately comment on the announcement.

The Justice Department’s move came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

The White House said on September 19 that covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”. The outlets ⁠sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.

CNN is one of the five ⁠news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – ⁠that make up the primary White House television pool.

They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage, and share the footage with outlets around the country.

All of the five television networks that cover the White House, including Fox ‌News, suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.

The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ‌ordered ‌the administration to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” their access.

However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued.

Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ Americas director, on Saturday criticised the administration’s decision to investigate.

“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

title: Five people shot and killed in apparent murder-suicide, Georgia police say
excerpt:
Deceased were all members of the same family, officials say, and one of victims placed the initial emergency call

Five people were shot and killed in an apparent murder-suicide at a residence in Geor...
body_text:
Deceased were all members of the same family, officials say, and one of victims placed the initial emergency call

Five people were shot and killed in an apparent murder-suicide at a residence in Georgia on Friday, authorities say.

The deceased were family members who lived at the home in Douglas, a city in south Georgia.

Officers responded to reports of an active shooter later on Friday, Brannen Pruette, the Douglas police chief, said at a Saturday news conference. One of the victims placed the initial emergency call.

Responding officers found four deceased adults inside the home. A fifth individual was transported to a hospital, where they were later pronounced dead.

Details around how the tragedy unfolded remain unclear, including who opened fire.

Hours before the deadly shooting, a female victim called police to complain that her husband was “killing her” with his smoking. EMS transported her to a local medical center.

Police did not offer additional information, citing the ongoing investigation.

“We recognize the profound impact this loss has on those closest to the victims in our community. We ask everyone to respect the privacy of the family and allow them the time and space they need to grieve,” Pruette said.

Charlie Davis, the Douglas city manager, said it was the area’s second murder-suicide incident in three months.

“Domestic violence doesn’t know race. It doesn’t know religion. It doesn’t know geographic location,” Davis said. “We encourage everyone to refrain from speculation and allow the family the space, dignity and compassion they deserve during this time.”

In a similar episode of violence, a man in Pennsylvania fatally shot several family members on Friday, before killing himself.

excerpt:

Keri Russell is getting candid about the early days in her relationship with her longtime ...
body_text:
Matthew Rhys told Fox News Digital that he plans on having a "wild" night after the 78th Annual Emmy Awards.

Keri Russell is getting candid about the early days in her relationship with her longtime partner.

During a recent appearance on the "Dear Chelsea" podcast, the 50-year-old actress discussed what it was like falling in love with her boyfriend, Matthew Rhys, while filming the early seasons of "The Americans."

"We were like falling in love and staying up all night and like having sex all the time and just like wearing disguises, like, I'm f---ing [in] crazy wigs and like wearing pearls," she said on the podcast. "When have you ever worn pearls and like, f---ing in trailers and f---ing everywhere. I mean, it was insanity. It was so fun and sneaky, and sexy, and so good."

Although the two had met briefly prior to working together, they reconnected in 2012 to film the first season of "The Americans" and their relationship became public in April 2014 after they first sparked dating rumors in late 2013.

Russell shared X-rated stories from the beginning of her and Rhys' relationship. (Dominik Bindl/WireImage)

Together they share their son Sam, who they welcomed in May 2016. Russell is also a mother to her two kids — River and Willa — from her previous marriage to Shane Deary.

While the couple have been together for over a decade, Russell told podcast host, Chelsea Handler, that she doesn't see the need to marry Rhys, noting, "I’ve had a big party. I get to dress up all the time."

"People used to have to be married to have a credit card. We can have credit cards now," Russell said. "I don’t need my last name to go away. I’m cool. If you wanna be here, be here. If you don’t, that’s cool too."

She added that since the two share a child, to her that means "forever" and that she finds marriage a bit "antiquated."

Rhys and Russell began dating while filming the first season of "The Americans." (Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty Images)

Russell is currently promoting the fourth season of her hit Netflix show, "The Diplomat," in which she portrays Kate Wyler, the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom who finds herself in the middle of conflicts between the two countries.

When it comes to the character, the "Felicity" actress told People, it is "fun to play someone so smart, so funny, so fierce," but who also "does stupid s--- all the time."

"I love her frankness, I love her bossiness. I love how she is always getting herself into hot water," she said. "I mean, to lose in a drama as a character is good. To be constantly losing and messing things up, it’s great. But I also love that she can pull it together and be presentable and put a dress on if she needs to."

After Rhys recently neglected to thank Russell in his acceptance speeches at the Emmy Awards, where he won for his work on both "Widow's Bay" and "The Beast In Me," Handler suggested that when Russell eventually wins for her role in "The Diplomat," she thanks all her ex-boyfriends and leaves Rhys out.

Russell explained she told Rhys he didn't have to thank her when he won an Emmy. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

While many were concerned by Rhys' omission, Russell explained she told him he didn't have to thank her, as he told her he was most nervous about having to make the speech if he won.

"I said, ‘Take me off your plate. Like, you don’t have to thank me. I know you love me,’" she revealed. There's so many people you have to thank. I don’t care if you want to thank the dog walker. You do whatever you want to do. That’s your minute. That’s your 45 seconds. So I just said, 'Take me off your plate.' And we kind of said to each other, 'We don’t have to thank each other.'"

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Unranked Oklahoma knocks off No. 1 Texas in walk-off fashion after Arch Manning's rough 4th quarter
excerpt:
OutKick's Trey Wallace provides an update on the weather after Hurricane Isaias' remnants made its way through Tuscaloosa ahead of Saturday's Alabama-Georgia game.

The top-ranked Texas Longhorns had ...
body_text:
OutKick's Trey Wallace provides an update on the weather after Hurricane Isaias' remnants made its way through Tuscaloosa ahead of Saturday's Alabama-Georgia game.

The top-ranked Texas Longhorns had at least a couple chances to win their third-straight Red River Rivalry, but the top-ranked team in the country faltered on its biggest stage of the college season.

Instead, the unranked Oklahoma Sooners took advantage of a missed field goal in the final minutes and two fourth-quarter interceptions by Arch Manning to pull off a wild 27-24 upset victory in Dallas.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Red River Rivalry looked like it would be all Texas early, as Arch Manning made one of his better plays, running to his left and throwing a 41-yard touchdown. Oklahoma matched it in the next quarter, but Texas was able to take a 17-7 lead at the half.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Oklahoma Sooners defensive back Peyton Bowen celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Texas Longhorns during the second half at Cotton Bowl in Dallas, Texas, on Oct. 10, 2026. (Kevin Jairaj/Imagn Images)

However, the Longhorns offense stalled, and the Sooners offense picked up in the fourth quarter. Oklahoma was able to squeak out a field goal in the third, while both teams exchanged punts, but the Sooners opened up the fourth quarter with a game-tying touchdown run by Lloyd Avant, erasing their double-digit deficit.

Both teams exchanged punts yet again, but on Texas’ second drive of the fourth quarter, Manning overthrew a receiver, and it was picked off by Peyton Bowen and taken to the house for a 42-yard pick-6, giving Oklahoma a 24-17 lead with 10:07 to go.

Oklahoma Sooners defensive back Dakoda Fields No. 9 celebrates after recovering a blocked punt by defensive lineman Danny Okoye No. 16 for a touchdown during the Allstate Red River Rivalry against the Texas Longhorns on Oct. 10, 2026, at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas, Texas. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

TULSA'S DAVID WELLS JR. TIPS BALL TO HIMSELF FOR IMPROBABLE TOUCHDOWN IN WILD PLAY AGAINST NAVY

Manning was down, but not out, as he hit Cam Coleman on a 342-yard dime to snatch all momentum. Manning found Jermaine Bishop Jr. two plays later to tie the score with 6:32 remaining. Texas then forced a punt after four plays and were in the driver's seat.

The Longhorns quickly got on the other side of the field, but they had to settle for a 52-yard field goal try - however, it went wide-right, and it was Oklahoma ball with 1:54 to go at their own 35. After forcing an Oklahoma punt, Texas had a shot to end the game in walk-off fashion, but Manning threw yet another fourth-quarter interception, ending that threat.

Oklahoma Sooners defensive lineman Trent Wilson (90) tackles Texas Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning (16) during the first half at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas, Texas, on Oct. 10, 2026. (Kevin Jairaj/Imagn Images)

Oklahoma got into field-goal range on back-to-back pass plays with nine seconds left, and Tate Sandell drilled a 47-yard field goal as time expired.
